title: Home and health over time
cando: say how long something has been true

about.text: In this lesson you talk about your home, your neighbours and your health. You say how long something has been true: I've lived here for six years. You read a notice in a building, and you talk to a doctor.
goals: Ask and answer: How long have you lived here? For six years. Since 2019.
Use for with a length of time, and since with the start.
Use somebody, nobody, everybody and everywhere.
Read a notice in a building and a short text about getting better.
Tell a doctor how long you have had a problem and what you have tried.

chapters.title: A new neighbour
chapters.text:
In this lesson you talk about time. Not when something happened, but how long.
First, you listen to two neighbours. Tomasz is new in the block. He moved in on Saturday.
Amina lives on the ground floor. Tomasz asks her: How long have you lived here?
Amina says: For six years. I've owned it since last summer.
Listen to for and since. In a sentence, for is short and quick. Since is clear.

chapters.title: for and since
chapters.text:
Amina came six years ago, and she still lives there. It started in the past, and it is still true now.
For this, use have or has and the past form. I have lived. She has worked. He has had.
Then use for or since. For goes with a length of time: for six years, for a week.
Since goes with the start: since 2019, since Monday.
To ask, say: How long have you lived here?
Do not say: I live here since 2019. Say: I've lived here since 2019.
You also learn somebody, nobody and everywhere. After everybody, the verb has an s: Everybody knows him.

chapters.title: A notice and a health text
chapters.text:
Next, you read a notice in the hall of a block of flats. The lift has not worked since Monday.
Then you read a short text: Getting better takes time. It explains an illness, an injury and treatment.
Then you write about your home. How long have you lived there? What is the area like?

chapters.title: At the doctor's
chapters.text:
In the task, you are at the doctor's. You have a painful knee.
The doctor asks: How long have you had it? You say: For three weeks.
The doctor asks: What have you tried? You say: I've rested it, and I've taken some tablets.
Then ask one question. Is it serious? How long will it take to get better?

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a story about home and health.
Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: A new neighbour moves into your building. What do you do?
choices: I say hello and tell them my name.
I smile, but I don't say anything.
I wait for them to say hello.
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. In many buildings, people say hello and give their name. A short chat on the stairs helps you get to know your neighbours.

conversation.title: A new neighbour
conversation.setting: Tomasz moved into a block of flats on Saturday. On Monday evening, he meets Amina in the hall.
lines: Amina
Hello! Are you the new tenant in flat 6?
Tomasz
Yes, that's right. I'm Tomasz. I moved in on Saturday.
Amina
Welcome to the block! I'm Amina. I'm on the ground floor.
Tomasz
Nice to meet you. How long have you lived here?
Amina
For six years. I rented my flat at first, but I've owned it since last summer.
Tomasz
So you know the area well. Is it a nice neighbourhood?
Amina
Yes, it's very peaceful. The street is never noisy at night.
Tomasz
Good! My last flat was above a café. It was so noisy.
Amina
Oh dear! Why did you choose this area?
Tomasz
I work at the local hospital. I've worked there since March.
Amina
Great! There's a good shop on the corner, too. Mr Khan has had it for twenty years. He knows everybody.
Tomasz
Thanks. I'd like to get to know people here.
Amina
Then come to the residents' meeting on Friday. Everybody is very friendly.

questions.q: How long has Amina lived in the block?
questions.why: Amina says: For six years. She has owned her flat since last summer.

questions.q: Why did Tomasz choose this area?
questions.a: He works at the local hospital.
wrong: His last flat was near here.
questions.why: Amina asks why he chose this area. Tomasz says: I work at the local hospital.

questions.q: What does Amina tell Tomasz to do on Friday?
questions.why: Amina says: Come to the residents' meeting on Friday.

phrases.text: How long have you lived here?
phrases.use: Asking about a length of time until now.
A length of time: use for.
Saying when you started to live in a new home.
Saying hello to a new neighbour.
Asking about the streets around a home.

phrases.text: I'd like to get to know people here.
phrases.use: Saying you want to meet your neighbours.

items.meaning: The streets around your home, and the people who live there.
items.example: I like this neighbourhood. The people are friendly.

items.meaning: A part of a town or a city.
items.example: Is there a good dentist in this area?

items.meaning: Near your home, or from the place where you live.
items.example: I buy my bread at the local bakery.

items.meaning: A big building with a lot of flats in it.
items.example: There are forty flats in our block.

items.meaning: A person who pays rent to live in a flat or a house.
items.example: The tenants pay the rent on the first day of the month.

items.meaning: Money you pay before you move in. You get it back at the end if nothing is broken.
items.example: I paid a deposit of £900 for the flat.

items.meaning: To start living in a new home.
items.example: We moved in last week, and there are still boxes everywhere.

items.meaning: A person who lives in a place, like a building or a town.
items.example: Only residents can park here.

items.meaning: The floor of a building at the same level as the street.
items.example: My flat is on the ground floor, so I don't need the lift.

items.meaning: With a lot of loud sounds.
items.example: Our street is noisy at night because of the bars.

items.meaning: Full of people.
items.example: The train to work is always crowded at eight o'clock.

items.meaning: Quiet, with no noise and no trouble.
items.example: The park is very peaceful in the early morning.

items.meaning: To spend time with people and learn more about them.
items.example: I got to know my neighbours at a street party.

items.meaning: To have something because it is yours. Often you bought it.
items.example: They don't own their flat. They rent it.

sound.title: for and since
sound.explain: In a sentence, for is short and quick. We don't say it strongly. Since is clear, with the sound in sit. Listen, then say each group.
groups: for six years · for a week · for a long time
lines: I've lived here for six years.
I've owned it since last summer.
How long have you worked there?

sayIt.instructions: Say these lines from the conversation. Record yourself, then listen back. Is your for short and your since clear?
lines: Nice to meet you. How long have you lived here?
For six years. I rented my flat at first, but I've owned it since last summer.
I work at the local hospital. I've worked there since March.
There's a good shop on the corner, too. Mr Khan has had it for twenty years.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. They all talk about a length of time until now.
examples: How long have you lived here?
I've owned it since last summer.
Mr Khan has had it for twenty years.
spot.question: What comes after for? What comes after since? Does Amina still live there?
spot.answer: After for: a length of time, like six years or twenty years. After since: the start, like last summer or March. The verb is have or has + the past form: have lived, has had. It started in the past, and it is still true now. So yes, Amina still lives there.

rules.title: for and since: How long have you …?
rule: have or has + the past form: I've lived here. She has worked there.
for + a length of time: for six years, for a week, for a long time.
since + the start: since 2019, since March, since Monday.
Ask: How long have you lived here? How long has he had his car?
Use it when something started in the past and is still true now.
rules.mistake: Not: I live here since 2019. Say: I've lived here since 2019.

rules.title: somebody, nobody, everybody, everywhere
rule: People: somebody (one person), everybody (all people), nobody (no people).
Places: somewhere (one place), everywhere (all places), nowhere (no place).
The verb is like he or she: Everybody knows Mr Khan. Nobody has called.
In questions and after not, use anybody and anywhere: Is anybody there?
Nobody already means not: Nobody came.
rules.mistake: Not: Nobody didn't come. Say: Nobody came.

practice.why: Six years is a length of time, so use for.

practice.q: She has worked at the hospital ___ March.
practice.why: March is the start, so use since.

practice.q: How long ___ you had this flat?
practice.why: How long + have you + the past form: How long have you had …?

practice.q: Tomasz ___ in the block since Saturday.
practice.why: It started on Saturday and is still true now: has lived.
2019 is the start, so use since.

practice.q: I ___ my car for ten years. It's old, but I love it.
practice.why: For + a length of time until now: have had.

practice.q: Everybody in the block ___ Mr Khan.
practice.why: Everybody takes a verb with s, like he or she: everybody knows.

practice.q: I knocked twice, but ___ answered. The flat was empty.
practice.why: The flat was empty, so not one person answered: nobody.

practice.q: I've looked ___ for my keys, but I can't find them.
___ has left a bag by the front door. Whose is it?
practice.why: One person, and we don't know who: somebody.

yourTurn.prompt: A new colleague wants to know about you. Write four sentences with for or since. Write about your home, your job, your phone and a friend.
yourTurn.model: I've lived in my flat for three years. I've worked at a hotel since 2022. I've had my phone for two years. I've known my best friend, Lena, since we were at school.

text.title: A notice in the hall, and Getting better takes time
text.body:
PRACTICE NOTICE: this building does not exist

ROSEWOOD COURT: NOTICE TO ALL RESIDENTS
12 March

THE LIFT
The lift has not worked since Monday 10 March. We are sorry. The problem is temporary. An engineer is coming on Friday to fix it. Until then, please use the stairs.

THE BINS
The bins are behind the building. Somebody has left old boxes next to them. Please do not leave anything there.

THE CAR PARK
The car park is now for residents only. This change is permanent.

Questions? Call the office on 01632 960 214, Monday to Friday, 9 am to 5 pm.

- - - - - - - -

GETTING BETTER TAKES TIME
Practice text: general information, not medical advice

An illness and an injury are different. An illness, like flu, is a problem inside your body. An injury comes from an accident, like a cut or a broken arm.
A doctor often asks: How long have you had this problem? A pain for two days and a pain for two months are not the same.
Treatment can be rest, medicine or exercises. Some people recover in a few days. Others need a longer period. A painful back can take weeks.
Everybody is different. If you don't feel better, go back to your doctor.

gist.a: problems and changes in a building
gist.why: The notice talks about the lift, the bins and the car park.

gist.q: What is the main idea of Getting better takes time?
gist.a: People need different times to get better.
wrong: Medicine always works in two days.
An injury is worse than an illness.
gist.why: The text says: Some people recover in a few days. Others need a longer period.

detail.q: How long has the lift been broken?
detail.why: The notice says: The lift has not worked since Monday 10 March.

detail.q: What is the problem with the bins?
detail.a: Somebody has left boxes next to them.
wrong: They are in front of the building.
detail.why: The notice says: Somebody has left old boxes next to them.

detail.a: The car park is for residents only.
wrong: There are boxes next to the bins.
detail.why: The notice says: The car park is now for residents only. This change is permanent.

detail.a: damage to your body from an accident
detail.why: An injury comes from an accident, like a cut or a broken arm.

items.meaning: For a short time only. It will stop or change soon.
items.example: I've got a temporary job in a hotel for the summer.

items.meaning: For a very long time, or for ever. It will not change.
items.example: After six months, my job became permanent.

items.meaning: You put your rubbish in it.
items.example: Please put your rubbish in the bin, not next to it.

items.meaning: To make something work again after it breaks.
items.example: The landlord fixed the heating yesterday.

items.meaning: A problem inside your body that makes you ill, like flu.
items.example: He was off work for two weeks because of an illness.

items.meaning: Damage to your body from an accident, like a cut or a broken arm.
items.example: She hurt her back at work. The injury took a month to get better.

items.meaning: What a doctor or a nurse does to help you get better.
items.example: The treatment is two tablets a day for a week.

items.meaning: To get well again after an illness or an injury.
items.example: He has recovered from his injury, and he's back at work.

items.meaning: A length of time.
items.example: The job is for a period of six months.

items.meaning: It hurts a lot.
items.example: My back is painful when I sit for a long time.

model.title: About my home
model.body:
I live in a flat on the second floor of a big block. I've lived here for four years.
The area is quite noisy, but the local shops are great.
I've known my neighbour, Lena, since I moved in. She's very friendly.
At the moment the heating isn't working, but that's temporary. The landlord is going to fix it on Monday.
I like my home, and I'd like to stay here for a long time.

write.task: Write about your home. It can be real or made up. Say how long you have lived there and what the area is like. Add one problem or one good thing.
write.starter: I live in … I've lived here for …
checklist: I used for or since at least twice.
I said what the area is like: peaceful, noisy, crowded …
I wrote about one problem or one good thing.
I used have or has + the past form: I've lived, I've known.

card.title: At the doctor's
card.situation: You've had a painful knee for three weeks. It started after a run in the park. You've tried rest and tablets from the chemist, but it still hurts on the stairs.
card.goal: Tell the doctor what is wrong and how long you have had it. Say what you have tried. Then ask one question.

phrases: I've had a pain in my knee for three weeks.
It started after a run in the park.
It's worse in the morning and on the stairs.
I've rested it, and I've taken some tablets.
How long will it take to get better?
prepare.notes: Make notes. What is wrong? How long have you had it? What have you tried? Write one question for the doctor.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is the doctor. Explain your problem, how long you have had it and what you have tried. Then change roles.
doIt.wehel: You are a doctor at a clinic. I am your patient. Ask me what the problem is and how long I have had it. Ask what I have tried. Then give me some simple advice. Use simple English.

model.title: The appointment
lines: Doctor
Good morning. Come in and sit down. What's the problem?
You
I've got a pain in my knee.
Doctor
I see. How long have you had it?
You
For about three weeks. It started after a run in the park.
Doctor
Is it painful all the time?
You
No, only on the stairs and in the morning.
Doctor
What have you tried?
You
I've rested it, and I've taken some tablets from the chemist.
Doctor
Have they helped?
You
A little, but it still hurts. Is it serious?
Doctor
I don't think so. It's a small injury. The treatment is some easy exercises.
You
How long will it take to get better?
Doctor
Most people recover in about a month. Come back if it gets worse.
You
OK. Thank you, doctor.
compare: Did you say how long you have had the problem, with for or since?
Did you say what you have tried: I've rested it, I've taken …?
Did you say when it hurts?
Did you ask a question: Is it serious? How long will it take?

canDo: I can ask and answer How long have you …?
I can use for with a length of time and since with the start.
I can talk about my home and my neighbourhood.
I can read a notice in a building and a short health text.
I can tell a doctor about a problem: how long, and what I have tried.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first picture. Where are the people? What do you think has changed in their life?
reading.talk: How long have the people in the story lived or worked there? And you? Write two or three sentences with for or since, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.why: 2020 is the start, so use since.

quiz.q: How long ___ she worked at the hospital?
quiz.why: How long + has she + the past form: How long has she worked …?

quiz.q: We've had our car ___ five years.
quiz.why: Five years is a length of time, so use for.

quiz.q: A person who pays rent to live in a flat is a ___ .
quiz.why: A tenant pays rent. A landlord owns the flat and gets the rent.

quiz.q: The lift is broken, but it's ___ . It will work again on Friday.
quiz.why: Temporary means for a short time only.

quiz.q: The market is very ___ on Saturdays. There are people everywhere.
I ___ Priya on Tuesday at ten. It's in my diary.
quiz.why: A plan with a day and a time: am + verb + -ing.

quiz.q: I was waiting for the bus when my phone ___ .
quiz.why: The short action that stopped the waiting: rang, the past of ring.

quiz.q: This phone is ___ useful than my old one.
quiz.why: Two things, a long word: more useful than.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the new neighbour conversation in pairs. Then change the facts: a new flat, a new job, a new town. Listen for a short for and a clear since.
Day 2: a how-long chain. Each learner asks the next one a question: How long have you lived here? How long have you had your phone? Then play a quick game with somebody, nobody and everywhere.
Day 3: the task. You are the doctor. Each learner explains a problem, how long they have had it and what they have tried. Then learners change roles.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and let two learners read their writing about their home aloud.
